summary: Describes UTF-7, a transformation format of Unicode that uses only 7-bit ASCII characters and is readable by humans when text is mostly US-ASCII. It is an experimental protocol. It was replaced by RFC 2152.

eli5.summary: A way to write many alphabets using only simple letters so old email systems do not break. A newer version replaced it.

questions: why is 7-bit encoding needed for email
how does utf-7 handle unicode in mail
subtitle: Encoding Unicode in 7-bit ASCII for email and old systems

tldr.problem: Internet mail systems only support 7-bit ASCII, but the world has many alphabets and symbols. Unicode can represent them all, but needs encoding for 7-bit mail.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-7 keeps ASCII text readable as-is, and uses shift sequences (starting with '+') to encode non-ASCII Unicode characters in a compact Modified Base64 format.
tldr.outcome: Email can now safely contain any Unicode character while remaining compatible with 7-bit mail systems and readable when it is mostly ASCII. RFC 2152 later improved the design.

today: RFC 1642 is experimental and was superseded by RFC 2152, which refined the encoding. However, UTF-7 is rarely used today. Modern systems prefer UTF-8 or full Unicode support, and MIME-8bit content transfer encoding eliminates the pressure to use 7-bit encodings.

sections.title: Unicode in 7-Bit Mail
sections.content:
Internet mail (RFC 822) is restricted to 7-bit US-ASCII characters. Unicode, the international standard for representing the world's writing systems, is a 16-bit character set covering more than 65,000 characters. MIME extended mail to support other character sets and content types, but it did not specify how to encode Unicode itself. UTF-7 solves this by transforming any Unicode character into 7-bit ASCII characters, making it safe for mail systems.

Other Unicode encodings like UTF-8 use bytes above 127, which are unsafe in 7-bit mail and must themselves be encoded with MIME content transfer encodings (like Base64 or Quoted-Printable). This double encoding wastes space. UTF-7 keeps ASCII text readable and unencoded, using only 7-bit ASCII throughout, so it works directly in mail without a second encoding step.
sections.eli5: Old email only understands letters A-Z, 0-9, and a few symbols. Unicode has Greek letters, Chinese characters, and emoji. UTF-7 is a code that lets you write those fancy things using only the letters email understands.

sections.title: How UTF-7 Works
sections.content:
UTF-7 has three simple rules. Rule 1: Direct encoding. ASCII letters (A-Z, a-z), digits (0-9), and a few safe punctuation marks (like '.' '-' ',' '/' ':' '?') are encoded as themselves. Optional characters like '@' and '[' can be directly encoded too, but some mail systems strip them.

Rule 2: Shifted encoding. Any other Unicode character is encoded using a shift sequence. The '+' character (US-ASCII 43) signals the start of special encoding. What follows is in a Modified Base64 alphabet (like the Base64 encoding in MIME, but without the '=' padding). The sequence ends either with '-' (which is consumed) or any non-Base64 character (which is processed normally). For instance, the smiley face 😊 (Unicode U+263A) is encoded as '+Jjo-' and the Japanese word 'nihongo' (U+65E5 U+672C U+8A9E) is '+ZeVnLIqe-'. ASCII text mixed with these sequences remains readable.

Rule 3: Whitespace. Space, tab, carriage return, and line feed are directly represented, though they must conform to MIME rules about line length and breaks.
sections.eli5: The code is simple: if it is a plain letter, keep it. If it is fancy, put '+', then encode it in a special alphabet, then put '-' to say we are done. English text in a message stays readable: 'Hi Mom +Jjo-!' is easy to see.

sections.title: Space Efficiency and Compatibility
sections.content:
UTF-7 is more efficient than alternatives. For text that is mostly ASCII (like most English email with a few accented letters or symbols), UTF-7 uses one octet per ASCII character and avoids the overhead of a second encoding layer. For non-ASCII characters, the average is about 2.67 octets per character plus a single shift overhead. By comparison, UTF-8 encoded in Base64 uses 1.33 octets per character for all text, rising to 4 octets for non-Western scripts. Quoted-Printable encoding of UTF-8 is even worse for non-Latin scripts.

UTF-7 is designed for 7-bit transports like mail and Usenet news. It is not suitable for binary protocols, where plain Unicode or UTF-8 is preferred. MIME declares UTF-7 text with charset=UNICODE-1-1-UTF-7. The encoding is safe for both the 7-bit content transfer encoding and the Q encoding used in mail headers, making it universally compatible with 7-bit systems.
sections.eli5: UTF-7 takes less space than other ways of sending Unicode in email, especially for mixed English and foreign text. It works on any email system, old or new, because it only uses the seven basic bits.

sections.title: Real-World Examples
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples that show how readable UTF-7 text can be. A+ImIDkQ. is the sequence for the mathematical symbols A, ≢ (NOT IDENTICAL TO), and Α (Greek alpha), followed by a period. Hi Mom +Jjo-! encodes 'Hi Mom', a white smiling face emoji, and an exclamation mark. A long document in Chinese shows how UTF-7 compresses whole sentences of Han characters into short Base64 sequences like +ZeVnLIqe- for 'nihongo' (the Japanese word for 'Japanese language'). Mixed text like Item 3 is +AKM-1. encodes the British pound sign (£) in the middle of an English sentence, keeping the English parts in clear text.

Care must be taken not to break shifted sequences across line boundaries. UTF-7 encoding should happen after line-breaking, or line-breaking and UTF-7 encoding should occur together. If a line becomes too long, MIME content transfer encodings like Quoted-Printable can apply a second layer of protection while preserving the UTF-7 structure.
sections.eli5: You can write 'Hi Mom +Jjo-!' and anyone without Unicode support still reads 'Hi Mom' and only sees garbage for the smiley face. Chinese text becomes short codes like '+ZeVnLIqe-'. The examples show this works in real messages.
